text.tspan: There are two things you should note about example 7. First, the technology computed the test statistic
and P-Value for us, which was a fabulous shortcut! Second, even though the P-Value was less than 0.05,
we did NOT reject the null hypothesis because for this problem the significance was 0.01. The default
level of significance is 5%, but if the consequences of a Type I error are severe, you may choose to use a
We are now ready to test hypotheses with context. We will test the first example twice, once using the
six-step process for those using only a probability calculator, and second using a t-test in STATBELT.
According to the most recent report from the Student Watch (funded by the National Association of College
Stores Foundation) the average cost for course materials (textbooks, electronic subscriptions, etc.) was $456
per course during the 2020-2021 academic year. An independent researcher decided to see if the costs have
declined going into the 2022-2023 academic year. They obtain a sample of 48 randomly selected students
with a sample mean course materials cost of $339 and standard deviation $207. Test the researcher’s claim
at the 0.01 significance level. Have the costs for course materials decreased?
In context, we are asked if there is enough evidence to conclude that the average (mean) cost has
declined. We will use a hypothesis test for a mean to evaluate the claim.
: We are given the average cost for course materials in 2020-2021 was $456 per course. The
in this case is referring to the mean. So, the null hypothesis is that the mean is
unchanged. The independent researcher believes the cost has declined (is now less than $456)
and collects data to try to prove it. This is the alternative hypothesis, making it a left tailed test.
We are asked to use significance level 0.01.
